definitions.example_sentence_native_language: As for the answer, I’ll give it to you tomorrow.

definitions.note: informal/polite spoken style (해요체)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If you have a question, answer right away.

definitions.note: Often used with the pattern “~(으)ㄴ/는 대로” meaning “as; just like; according to.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please do it the way I said.

definitions.note: Often used with “~ 대신(에)” meaning “instead of (doing something).”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I drank tea instead of coffee.

definitions.note: Often used for an organized group (e.g., a marching line or ranks).
Used to express annoyance, surprise, or emphasis in questions (similar to “what on earth?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Why on earth are you so late?

definitions.note: Often used to add emphasis in questions (e.g., 대체 왜…?); can sound frustrated or surprised.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Why on earth are you so late?

definitions.note: Comes from the verb 대하다 (“to deal with; to face”) and is used as a modifier meaning “about/regarding,” often before nouns like 문제 (issue), 이야기 (story), 설명 (explanation).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: We need an explanation about this problem.

definitions.note: Adnominal form of 대하다, used before a noun (e.g. “~에 대한 + noun” = “a noun about ~”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I read a book about the environment.

definitions.note: Used after a noun as in “~에 대해” (“about/regarding ~”).
Often used with -에 대해 to mean “about/regarding.”
From 대하다 (“to treat/deal with”); can describe how you treat a person.
Used after a noun as in “~에 대해서” (“about/regarding ~”).
Object form of 대화 (used with 를).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I had a conversation with a friend.

definitions.note: Used to mean an increased degree or amount; often combines with words like "더 많이" (more), "더 좋아" (better).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I want to drink more water.

definitions.note: Attributive (modifier) form of 더럽다; used before a noun.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please don't touch the food with dirty hands.

definitions.note: Often used in negative sentences (e.g., with 안/못/없다). Also commonly written as '더 이상' with a space.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 저는 더이상 그 사람을 만나지 않아요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I don't meet that person anymore.

definitions.note: Used to say something happened because of someone/something (often with a positive meaning).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 당신 덕분에 한국어를 더 열심히 공부하게 됐어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Thanks to you, I ended up studying Korean harder.

definitions.note: Informal/plain style; often used as a command (“Throw it!”) or as the verb stem before endings (e.g., 던져요).

definitions.native: come at me, bring it on
definitions.note: Informal imperative of 덤비다; often sounds aggressive or challenging.
A dependent noun used after a verb/adjective phrase to mean “the place/thing/situation (where/that…)”. Often appears in patterns like “-(으)ㄹ 데” (a place/way to do).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I don’t have anywhere to go today.

definitions.note: Often used as an imperative/informal command meaning “Take them/it with you.”
Used to describe something/someone that is taking a person along (attributive form of 데려가다).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My dad is taking me to the park.

definitions.native: will take (someone) (with you), going to bring (someone)
definitions.note: Used before a noun (e.g., 데려갈 사람 ‘the person (I) will take’) or before 것/거 to mean ‘going to take (someone)’.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The person I'm going to take with me tomorrow is my younger sibling.

definitions.native: take (someone) (to a place), bring (someone) (to a place)
definitions.note: Often used before another verb (especially 주다) to mean “take/bring (someone) somewhere (for them).”
Used after a noun or pronoun to mean “together with,” especially when taking or bringing a person (e.g., 데리고 가다 “take/bring someone”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I went to the hospital with my younger sibling (bringing them along).

definitions.note: Short for "데 + 에서". Used after a describing phrase or clause to mean “at/in/from where (something happens)” or “at the place where.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I waited at a place where there were a lot of people.

definitions.note: Added after a noun/pronoun (or after the topic/subject particle) to mean “also/too.”
Can emphasize something as surprising or unexpected, often with negative statements.

definitions.native: on earth, in the world, what in the world
definitions.note: Used to add emphasis, often in questions or when complaining (similar to “what on earth…?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: What on earth is going on?

definitions.note: informal command (casual speech), like “Run away!”
Informal/casual command form ("Run away!") of 도망치다.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It's dangerous, so run away now!

definitions.note: Future modifier form used before a noun (e.g., “a person who will run away”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I didn't have a chance to run away.

definitions.native: as for the city, the city (topic)
definitions.note: "도시" (city) + topic marker "-는".
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: As for the city, there are really a lot of people.

definitions.note: Direct object form of 도시 (“city”), used before a verb.
‘도시’ (city) + the location particle ‘-에서’ (in/at; where an action happens).
Casual/informal command or request (from 돕다). Often used like “Help (me)!”

definitions.native: have to help, need to help
definitions.note: Often followed by 돼요/된다 to mean “have to.”
Modifier form of the verb 돕다 (“to help”); used before a noun (like an adjective).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 저는 사람들을 도와주는 일을 하고 싶어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I want to do work that helps people.

definitions.note: Often used before a noun to mean “that/who will help,” and can also be used as a casual sentence ending meaning “I’ll help.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: There’s someone here who will help you.

definitions.note: informal request (to a friend/someone younger)
Future/intent form of 돕다 used before a noun (e.g., “도울 사람” = “a person who will help”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m looking for someone to help.

definitions.note: Object form of 도움, used before object markers like -을/를 (e.g., 도움을 받다/주다).
“도움이” is “도움” + the subject marker “-이” (meaning “help” as the subject of the sentence).
Usually means an official stamp/seal used on documents (often with ink).
Object-marking form of 도장 (도장을). Can mean a rubber stamp/seal, or a personal name seal used to officially sign documents.
past tense of 도착하다
독은 is 독 (“poison”) with the topic particle -은 (“as for…”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Poison is harmful to the body.
He put poison in the water.

definitions.note: Often refers to a traditional Korean ceramic jar used for foods like soy sauce or doenjang (e.g., 된장독).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Grandma stores doenjang in an earthenware jar.

definitions.note: From the noun 독 (“poison/toxin”) with the subject marker -이.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This mushroom has poison in it.

definitions.note: 도 means “also/too,” attached to 돈 (“money”). Often implies “even money (too)” depending on context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I don’t have time, and I don’t have money either.

definitions.note: ‘돈은’ means “as for money” or “money (topic marker)” (돈 + 은).
The object form of 돈 (“money”), used before a verb.
돈 with the subject marker -이 (used after a consonant).
Casual/informal form of 돌리다, used with friends or in casual speech.
Casual/informal form of 돌리다, often used when asking someone to give something back.
Informal (casual) request/command form.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Give me back my book, please.

definitions.note: Informal present form of 돌다; can also be used as an informal command depending on context.
Often used for going back (to a place) or returning (home).
The -고 ending links to the next clause, like “and/then.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I want to go back home.

definitions.note: Modifier (attributive) form of 돌아가다 used to describe a noun (e.g., ‘the returning bus’).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I bought bread on the way back.

definitions.native: have to go back, must return
definitions.note: Used to say it is necessary to go back/return (like “should/must”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I have to go home now.

definitions.note: Future/likely form of 돌아가다 (“to go back/return”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I will go back home tomorrow.

definitions.note: This is the future attributive form of 돌아오다, used to describe a noun (e.g., ‘the person who will come back’).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please tell me what time you will come back.

definitions.note: Used to connect actions: ‘come back and then…’ (from 돌아오다 + -아서/어서).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I came back home and then ate dinner.
He came back home late yesterday.

definitions.note: past tense of 돌아오다 (to come back)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I came back home from the trip yesterday.

definitions.note: informal, past tense (used in casual speech)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I just came back home now.

definitions.note: Used to link to a following verb/action (…돕고 …).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I helped my friend and we did homework together.

definitions.note: Used in forms like 돕지 않다 (do not help) or 돕지? (Help, won’t you?) depending on context.

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: There are many animals at the zoo.

definitions.note: ‘은’ is the topic particle used after nouns ending in a consonant (like 동물).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: As for animals, they usually have four legs.

definitions.note: The object-marked form of 동물 (with 를).
This is 동물 + subject particle 이 (“animal” as the subject of the sentence).
informal/polite-low ending used in casual speech; often translates as “(it’s) an animal.”
Used for a younger brother or younger sister (relative to the speaker).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My younger sibling goes to school.

definitions.note: Used with the object particle -을, so it marks “younger sibling” as the direct object in the sentence.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I really like my younger sibling.

definitions.note: Possessive form of 동생 (“younger sibling”), used before a noun.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My younger sibling's room is on the second floor.
The two people opened the door at the same time.

definitions.note: Used after a time expression to mean “during” or “for (a period of time)”.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I was in Korea during vacation.

definitions.note: used after a time expression to mean “during/for that period.” Often in forms like ~동안에 (during) or ~동안 (for).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I was in Korea during summer vacation.

definitions.note: commonly used in the phrase 동안이다 (“to look young for one’s age”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My older sister really has a baby face.

definitions.note: casual/informal form, often used in phrases like -아/어도 돼 (“it’s okay to …”)
Informal spoken form of 되다, commonly used to mean something is okay/allowed/possible.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Is it okay if I do this?

definitions.note: Polite informal form used to say something is allowed/acceptable or possible (often in patterns like ~아/어도 돼요).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You can go now (It's okay to go now).

definitions.note: Polite casual form of 되다; used to mean something is allowed/possible or acceptable.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Is it okay if I do it now?

definitions.native: did it work?, is it done?
definitions.note: Casual question form of 되다 (“to become; to work out”), often used when checking whether something has been completed or succeeded.
Past tense of 되다; often used to say something is finished or acceptable (like “Okay, done.”).

definitions.native: it’s done, it worked, it’s okay
definitions.note: Casual/informal past form of 되다; often used to mean “it worked/it’s done” or “okay, that’s enough/stop.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It’s okay now. Let’s go home.

definitions.note: Casual (informal) past form of 되다. Often used to mean “okay/that’s enough” or “it’s settled.”

definitions.native: it worked, it’s done, it’s 됐어요 (it’s fine/okay)
definitions.note: Common past polite form of 되다. Often used as a response meaning “it’s fine/okay” or “no thanks,” depending on context.
Contraction of "되었죠" (past tense of 되다 + the polite ending "-지요"), often used to confirm something or expect agreement.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The reservation is done now, right?

definitions.note: Informal. Past tense of 되다 with -지, often used to confirm something or seek agreement (like “right?” / “see?”).

definitions.native: will it work?, do you think it will work?
definitions.note: Informal question form; often used rhetorically to express doubt ("Do you really think that’ll work?").
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Do you think it’ll work if you do it like that?

definitions.native: will it work?, would it be okay?
definitions.note: formal/polite question, often used to ask if something is acceptable or possible
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Would it be okay if we start now?

definitions.note: Connective form of 되다 with -고 (“and”), used to link to the next clause (often in phrases like ~되고 싶다, “want to become”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I want to become a teacher.

definitions.native: is it possible?, does it work?, is it okay?
definitions.note: Used as a polite question ("되다" + "-나요") asking whether something is possible/allowed or whether something works.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Can I pay by card here?

definitions.native: does it work?, is it okay?, is it possible?
definitions.note: Polite question form of 되다, used to ask if something is okay/allowed/possible or if something works.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Is it okay to take pictures here?

definitions.note: Adnominal (noun-modifying) form of the auxiliary 되다, used after a verb stem to mean something can be done or works.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 이 방법은 누구나 쉽게 따라 할 수 있는, 되는 방법이에요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This method is a doable method that anyone can easily follow.

definitions.note: Attributive (modifier) form of 되다 used before a noun.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 이 방법이 제일 잘 되는 방법이에요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This method is the one that works best.

definitions.note: Connector ending -는데 added to 되다; often sets background or contrast, like “but/though …”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It works now, but it won’t tomorrow.

definitions.note: From 되다 (“to become; to be okay/work”), used with -면 to mean “if/when …”.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If I have time, I'll call you.

definitions.note: Polite request form of 되다. Very commonly used in set phrases like “좋은 하루 되세요” (= have a nice day).
Conjugated form of 되다 used to connect to the next clause (like “becoming… / and then…”), or as “되어” in passive/causative-style expressions.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I went to Korea after becoming an adult.

definitions.note: past tense (plain style) of 되다; often used meaning “it ended up being/it turned out to be.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: In the end, the appointment got canceled.

definitions.note: Contraction of "되지요"; often used to confirm or soften a statement (like “it works, right?” / “it should be okay, right?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If I do it like this, it works, right?

definitions.note: Polite conversational ending (short for 되지요) often used to confirm or seek agreement, like “right?”
Often used in questions or negatives like “되지?” (Is it okay?/Does it work?) or “안 되지” (It won’t work / It’s not allowed).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If I do it like this, is it okay?

definitions.note: Past attributive form of 되다, used before a noun to mean “that became” or “that is done/finished.”
Present tense plain (dictionary-style) form of 되다; often used to mean something is acceptable/allowed or that something works.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This method works. It works well.

definitions.native: that it works, that it will be (possible)
definitions.note: Used to quote or report a statement with -(ㄴ)다고 (e.g. “(someone) says that…” / “(someone) said that…”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My friend said that this method works.

definitions.native: if it works out, if it becomes (that way)
definitions.note: Conditional form of 되다 used to mean “if it turns out that…” or “if it works out…”, depending on context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If you have time, let’s eat lunch together.

definitions.note: Future attributive form of 되다 used before a noun (e.g., 될 사람 “a person who will become…”).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 그는 우리 팀의 리더가 될 사람이에요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He is the person who will become our team’s leader.

definitions.note: future attributive form of 되다; used before a noun (e.g. ‘될 + N’ = ‘a N that will be/become’)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He is someone who will soon become a doctor.

definitions.note: Contraction of "될 거야" (informal). Used to say something will happen or become true in the future.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Tomorrow will get busier, but it’ll be okay.

definitions.native: will it work?, will it happen?
definitions.note: Used to wonder about a possibility or outcome; often expresses uncertainty.

definitions.native: will it work?, will it be okay?
definitions.note: Used to wonder or ask if something will be possible or acceptable.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Will it work if I do it like this?

definitions.native: will it work?, will it be?
definitions.note: Used to wonder or ask if something will happen or be possible (되다 + -(으)ㄹ까).

definitions.native: will it be okay?, will it work?
definitions.note: Polite question used to check if something is acceptable/possible, or to ask for confirmation.

definitions.native: will it work?, will it be okay?
definitions.note: Polite question form used to ask if something is possible/okay (often like “would it be okay if…?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Would it be okay if I sit here?

definitions.native: is it possible?, does it work?, is it done?
definitions.note: Formal polite question form of 되다; used to ask if something is okay/allowed/possible or if something works out.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Is it okay to take pictures here?

definitions.note: Formal polite style. Often used in polite statements like “It’s okay/possible” or “This works.”
Polite/formal present tense of 되다; often used to mean something is possible/allowed or that something works/has been done.
native Korean number used before a noun/counter (attributive form of 둘)
Connective form of 두다 used to link clauses (often meaning “after leaving/putting …”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I left the door open and went out.

definitions.note: Noun + subject marker (-이).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 두려움이 너무 커서 아무것도 못 했어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My fear was so big that I couldn’t do anything.

definitions.note: Informal/casual form of 두렵다, often used before a following clause (e.g., “두려워서…” = “because I’m afraid…”).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 저는 혼자 밤에 걷는 게 두려워요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m afraid to walk alone at night.

definitions.note: Often used before an ending like 않아/않아 (e.g., 두렵지 않아 = “I’m not afraid”) or as a casual question (두렵지? = “Aren’t you afraid?”).
두통 means “headache.” 두통이 is used when “headache” is the subject (with the subject particle -이).
Modifier form of 두다 used before a noun (e.g., 둘 곳 = “a place to put (something)”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: There’s nowhere to put this luggage.

definitions.note: native Korean numeral (used before counters; e.g., 둘, 셋, 넷)
‘둘’ means “two (people/things)”; ‘-은’ marks it as the topic (“as for the two…”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The two of them are friends.

definitions.note: Used when talking about two people/things as the subject (둘 + subject particle 이).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The two of them went to see a movie together.

definitions.native: leave (it) (done), do and keep (it that way)
definitions.note: Contraction of 두어 in the auxiliary pattern -아/어 두다, meaning you do something and leave it in that state (often ‘do in advance’).
Informal form of 두다, often used as a command ("Put it/Leave it").
Often used with verbs of movement to mean going to the back or moving backward.
Used to indicate a position/time that comes after another person/thing/event; commonly used with a noun + 뒤에.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The bag is behind the chair.

definitions.native: behind, in back of; after, later
definitions.note: 뒤에 is 뒤 (“back/behind”) + the location/time particle 에 (“at/in/on”), so it can mean both a place (“behind”) and a time (“after”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: There is a park behind the school.

definitions.note: Humble/polite form used when offering to do something for the listener (from 드리다).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Shall I carry your bag for you?

definitions.native: shall I give it to you?, would you like me to give it to you?
definitions.note: Polite offer/question form of 드리다 (“to give (to someone respected)”). Often used when offering help or handing something to someone.

definitions.native: please eat, please have (some), please take (it)
definitions.note: Polite imperative/honorific form used when asking someone (often older or a customer) to eat or take something.
Connects to the next verb/clause, meaning “and then/and (while) …” (verb stem + -고).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I listen to music and study.

definitions.note: Used with the ending -지 (often followed by 않다/못하다/마(요)), e.g. 듣지 마(요) = “don’t listen.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please don’t listen to music right now.

definitions.note: From 들다 (“to hold, lift, carry”); -고 links to the next verb or clause (“and/while”), so 들고 often means “holding/carrying (and then…)”.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I went home carrying a bag.

definitions.note: From 들리다 (“to be heard; to be audible”). Often used to say something is audible or that you can hear something.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You can hear the music well from here.

definitions.note: Casual/questioning ending -나; often sounds rhetorical or like talking to oneself. From 들리다 (“to be heard”).
Very informal, casual question form of 들리다 (“to be heard”). Often used like “You hear me?”
casual/informal form (can be used as a command like “listen!” or as casual speech like “(I) hear/listen.”)
Informal present form; also used as a casual command meaning “come in.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Is it okay if I come in? Come in.

definitions.note: Often used as an informal command meaning “Go in/Go inside.”
Often used as an informal command meaning “go in/come in.”

definitions.native: even if (someone/something) goes in, even if (someone/something) enters
definitions.note: From 들어가다 + -아/어도 (“even if / even though”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Is it okay if I go in now?

definitions.note: polite present tense (요 form); can also be used like “go (ahead) inside” depending on context
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m going into the house now.

definitions.note: Future modifier form of 들어가다; used before a noun (e.g., 들어갈 곳 “a place to enter/go into”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Where is the room I will go into?

definitions.note: past tense of 들어가다
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He quietly went into the room.

definitions.native: have heard (of), have listened to before
definitions.note: Past modifier form used before a noun, meaning “that (someone) has heard/experienced before.”
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 이 노래는 전에 들어본 적이 있어요.

definitions.native: want to listen, want to try listening
definitions.note: Informal. Used to suggest or ask if someone wants to try listening to something.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Do you want to listen to this song (and see what you think)?

definitions.note: informal command (casual speech); often used like “listen (to me)” / “hear me out.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Listen to me for a second.

definitions.note: Polite present tense of 듣다.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m listening to music right now.

definitions.native: did you hear?, did you listen?
definitions.note: Informal past-tense question (to a friend/younger person).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Did you hear what I said?

An imperative command; very direct/harsh. Can also be used in fiction as an order (e.g., “Kill him/her/them”).
This form combines 죽이다 + -어 버리다, often adding the feeling of doing it completely or with strong emotion. It can be used literally or as an exaggerated threat in casual speech.

definitions.note: From 죽이다 (“to kill”) + -아/어야 (“have to / must”). Depending on context it can also be used hyperbolically like “I could kill (someone)” in casual speech.

definitions.note: Past tense with the casual question ending -나; often used in informal speech, sometimes as a self-directed question (“did I…?”).
casual/polite past tense (as in speech between friends)
Polite past tense of 죽이다 (“to kill”). It can also be used casually to mean “That was awesome/amazing,” depending on context.
Used before a noun to mean something/someone is dead (attributive form of 죽다).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I saw a dead bird on the street.

definitions.note: Attributive form of 죽다, used before a noun (e.g., “dead person”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: A dead fish is floating in the water.

definitions.note: Attributive (noun-modifying) form of 죽다, used before a noun.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He has an illness that will kill him.

definitions.note: Future attributive form of 죽다, used before a noun (e.g. 죽을 병 “a fatal illness”).
Question form using -을/ㄹ까 to wonder or ask about a possibility (often used when thinking to oneself or asking indirectly).
object-marked form of 죽음 (with 을), used when it is the direct object in a sentence
Connects to the next verb or clause, like “and then…”.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I killed the mosquito and closed the window.

definitions.note: From 죽이다 (“to kill”); 죽이는 is a modifier form used before a noun (e.g., “a killing blow”).

definitions.native: to try to kill, to be about to kill
definitions.note: From 죽이다 (“to kill”) + -(으)려 (“in order to / intending to”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He picked up a newspaper to kill the bug.

definitions.native: to try to kill, in order to kill
definitions.note: Used with -(으)려고 to express intention or purpose.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 그 남자는 나를 죽이려고 칼을 들었어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: That man picked up a knife to try to kill me.

definitions.note: Often used as a casual ending like “-지” to add emphasis, as in “죽이지!” = “It’s killer!” / “Awesome!” (not literal).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: That movie is seriously awesome, right?

definitions.note: Past attributive form of 죽이다, used to modify a noun (e.g., “the person (someone) killed”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He buried the animal he killed.

definitions.note: Often also used casually to mean something is amazing or very intense (e.g., 맛이 죽인다 = “it tastes incredible”).
Often used before a noun to mean “killer/amazing” (slang), but literally it means “to kill” as a modifier.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I don't have the strength to kill.

definitions.note: This is the verb 죽다 with the ending -지, commonly used before 않다 (not) or 말다 (don’t), e.g. 죽지 마(요) = “don’t die.”
Past attributive form of 주다, used before a noun.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I read the book you gave me.

definitions.note: “준비” (preparation) + subject particle “가”. Often used as “준비가 되다” (to be ready).
Informal casual speech. Often means “(I’m) ready” or “Are you ready?” depending on context.
Direct object form of 준비 with the particle 를.
Informal/polite spoken form of 준비하다 (as in 준비해요).

definitions.native: will do for (someone), will give (as a favor)
definitions.note: Used as the auxiliary form of 주다 after another verb to mean doing that action for someone (a favor/service). Often appears inside longer forms like -줄게요, -줄까요, -줄 수 있어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’ll carry your bag for you.

definitions.native: will give, to give (as a modifier)
definitions.note: Form of 주다 used before a noun (e.g. 줄 사람 “the person who will give”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This is a gift I’ll give you.
People are standing in a line.
I tied the box with a rope.

definitions.note: Used to ask oneself or someone for a suggestion/decision; often means “Should I give it to you?” depending on context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Should I give this to you?

definitions.native: should I give (it), shall I give (it)
definitions.note: Often used to offer something or ask for a suggestion; from 주다 (“to give”) + -ㄹ까 (“shall I?/should I?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Should I give you coffee? / Want some coffee?

definitions.note: Used to make a casual, friendly request. Often follows a verb stem (e.g., 해 줄래? "will you do it for me?") or 주다 "to give".
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Will you give me this, please?

definitions.native: will you (do it)?, can you (do it) for me?
definitions.note: Polite request form (often used after a verb stem), asking someone to do something for you.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Can you help me with this?

definitions.native: will you (do/give it)?, can you (do/give it)?
definitions.note: Polite request form, often translated as “will you…?” or “can you…?” depending on context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Can you give me some water?

definitions.native: as for the line, as for the string
definitions.note: ‘줄’ can mean a line/queue or a string/rope; ‘-은’ marks the topic (“as for…”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: As for the line, you can stand starting from here.

definitions.note: Used after a noun to mean something is currently happening (e.g., 회의 중 = during a meeting / in a meeting).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m in a meeting right now, so please don’t call.

definitions.native: in the middle of, in the process of
definitions.note: Used after a verb (usually with -는) to mean someone is currently doing something (e.g., 공부하는 중이에요 / 공부 중이에요).
Often used as a bound noun in patterns like “N 중(에/에서)” meaning “among N / out of N.”
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 세 명 중에 한 명이 학생이에요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Out of three people, one person is a student.

definitions.native: in the middle of, during (in progress)
definitions.note: Often used as a bound noun meaning something is currently happening (e.g., “회의 중” = “in a meeting”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m in a meeting right now.

definitions.note: This form includes the object particle 를, so it often marks “Chinese” as the direct object of a verb (e.g., learn, study, speak).
Used to describe an important or grave matter (e.g., a problem, decision, incident).
Often used to say something (a song, game, flavor, etc.) is hard to stop once you start.
Informal/casual speech (ending -야), used after a noun.
Used after a noun to mean “among/between (them).” (From the noun 중 “middle/among” + particle 에.)

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Among the three people, who is the tallest?

definitions.note: used to mean “among” a group or “out of” a set (often with superlatives or choices)
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 친구들 중에 누가 제일 키가 커요?
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Among your friends, who is the tallest?

definitions.note: used after a noun (often with a number/amount) to mean “among/out of (a group)”
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 세 명 중에서 한 명이 학생이에요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Out of three people, one is a student.

definitions.note: Used before a noun (attributive form of 중요하다).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I have an important meeting today.

definitions.note: Informal polite style ending; a common spoken form of 중요하다.

definitions.native: in the middle of, in the process of
definitions.note: Spoken, informal present tense of '중이다', used after a noun to mean 'in the middle of doing (something)' (e.g., 공부 중이야 = I'm studying).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I'm in the middle of doing my homework right now.

definitions.note: Used after a verb stem + -는 중이다 to mean an action is in progress; this is the polite form (-입니다).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m doing my homework right now.

definitions.note: Informal/casual request form of the auxiliary 주다 used after a verb (like -아/어 줘) to mean “please do it for me/someone.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please open the door for me.

definitions.note: informal command/request form of 주다; often used like “give me …” depending on context
From 주다 (“to give”) + -아/어야 (“have to / must”). Often used when saying someone is required to give something.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You have to give me the money by tomorrow.

definitions.note: Casual/polite (해체) past form of 주다 used as an auxiliary to show doing something for someone (often implying a favor).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I helped my friend with their homework (as a favor).

definitions.note: Informal/polite past tense of 주다 (“to give”). Often used when the object is understood from context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I gave my friend a present yesterday.

definitions.note: Can refer to either a small mouse or a rat depending on context (e.g., 집쥐 is a house rat).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: There is a mouse in the kitchen.

definitions.note: 쥐 is the animal; -가 is the subject particle attached to it.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: A mouse came into the room.

definitions.note: 쥐 + 를: the object form (accusative particle) of 쥐.
Attributive form of 즐겁다 used before a noun.
Adverb form of 즐겁다; often used with verbs like 지내다 (to spend time) or 하다 (to do).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I had fun playing with my friends.

definitions.note: ‘증거’ means “evidence/proof,” and ‘-가’ is the subject marker.
-는 is a topic marker attached to 증거 (“evidence”).
Future modifier form of 증명하다; used before a noun (e.g., ‘something to prove’).

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He is waiting for a chance to prove his skills.

definitions.note: Often used with a modifier, especially in terms like “A4지” (A4 paper).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please give me one sheet of A4 paper.

definitions.note: Used after a clause to make an indirect/embedded question.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Do you know where (they) are going?

definitions.note: Common in casual speech after a statement, similar to a tag question.

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: What are you doing right now?
Until now, nobody knew that fact.

definitions.note: Emphasizes that something is true even at the present time (often continuing from the past).
지금 (“now”) + topic particle 은; often used to mean “as for now / right now” depending on context.
used before a noun to refer to the time period before now (e.g., 지난주 = last week)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It rained a lot last week.

definitions.note: -에 is a particle meaning “in/on/at” (time/place), so 지난주에 means “last week” in the sense of “during last week.”

definitions.note: Often used with time expressions (e.g., 하루를 지내다) or with people (e.g., 잘 지내다 = be doing well / be getting along).

definitions.note: Commonly used to talk about how you are doing or how you’ve been spending your time (e.g., “How have you been?”).
Casual/informal past tense. Often used when talking about how you spent time or how things went (e.g., “How have you been?”).

Object form of 지역 (region/area), used with the object particle 을.

definitions.note: Object form of 지원 (used before verbs like 하다/받다/요청하다).

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The company gives support to new employees.

definitions.note: Often used as part of the verb phrase 지지하다 (“to support”), especially in forms like 지지해요/지지합니다.

definitions.note: Modifier form of 지키다; used before a noun (e.g., ‘the person who keeps/protects …’).

definitions.note: Conjugated form of 지키다 used to mean “will protect/keep” (or “to protect/keep” depending on context).

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Grandpa walked slowly using a cane.

definitions.note: 지하철 + 로 (“by/through”), indicating means or route.

definitions.note: Object form of 지하철 with the particle -을.

직업(occupation/job) + 은(topic marker). Often used to introduce or contrast the topic “job.”
직업 + object particle 을 (used when the noun is the object of a verb).

Object-marked form of 진실 with the particle 을.
Used to emphasize that you really mean something; often with apologies, thanks, or feelings.
Polite form often used as a request/command (e.g., to a customer, stranger, or someone you should be respectful to).

Honorific word used for an older person’s meal (like 밥/식사).
Often used in casual speech to mean “really?” / “for real?” or to emphasize something (like “seriously”).
Often used in casual speech for emphasis, like “seriously?” or “for real?” depending on context.
Often used in casual speech for emphasis, like “really?” or “seriously?” depending on context.
Often used to emphasize that something is real/serious, or to show surprise (like “really?”).
Casual/informal style (to friends, family).

‘집’ (house/home) + subject marker ‘-이’ (when the noun ends in a consonant).

Noun "짓" (act/deed) + topic particle "-은". Used to mark "짓" as the topic of the sentence.
Object form of the noun 짓 (with 을). Often used to mean a (bad) deed depending on context.

definitions.note: Colloquial; used to say that something isn’t true (often as a response).
often used after a noun to mean “the side/part of …” or “toward …” (e.g., 왼쪽 “left side”)
Used after a noun (often with a direction word like 오른쪽/왼쪽) to mean “toward/to that side.”

Often used to mean something continues without stopping (e.g., keep doing something) or goes in a straight line/direction.

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: When you go home, go straight on this road.

definitions.native: will find, to find (as in “find + -ㄹ/을” future/intent modifier)

definitions.native: in the book, to the book, on the book

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I'll take care of this problem by today.

definitions.native: from the beginning, from the start
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’ll start again from the beginning.

definitions.note: Commonly used in the pattern ‘-(으)ㄴ/는 척 (하다)’ to mean “pretend (to do/be)”.
From 척하다; used after a noun/phrase to mean “to act as if (it’s that way).”
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 괜찮은 척하는 거지, 사실은 많이 힘들어.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m just acting like I’m okay; actually, I’m having a really hard time.

definitions.note: This is the noun 천둥 (“thunder”) + the possessive particle -의 (“of”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The sound of thunder is too loud.

definitions.note: Used before a noun (e.g., 첫날 “first day”, 첫사랑 “first love”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Today is the first day of the new semester.

definitions.note: Used before a noun, as in 첫날 (first day), 첫 번째 (first).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Today is the first day of school.

definitions.native: at first sight, at a glance
definitions.note: Often used in the expression 첫눈에 반하다 (“to fall in love at first sight”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I recognized that person at first sight.

definitions.note: Casual/informal form of 치다 (used in everyday speech; can also be used as a casual command depending on context).
informal past tense of 치다; often used in casual speech
From 총 (gun) + 에 (at/in/to). Often used with verbs like 맞다 (to get hit) or 쏘다 (to shoot).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He was hit by a gunshot.

definitions.note: ‘총을’ is ‘총’ (gun) with the object particle -을.
An honorific title used to address or refer to a president (총통); often associated with Taiwan/Republic of China in modern usage.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: His Excellency the President gave a speech today.

definitions.note: Honorific particle (께) meaning 'to' used when the recipient is a respected person.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please deliver this letter to the president.

definitions.note: Used to refer respectfully to a president; 께서 is the honorific subject particle.
Used with the object particle -을 here (총통을). In modern Korean, 대통령 is more common; 총통 is used for some countries’ titles or in historical contexts.
Often used as a noun meaning “the best/the top,” or as an exclamation meaning “the best!”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This café has the best coffee.

definitions.native: is the best, are the best
definitions.note: Casual/informal ending (often said to friends). Can mean “It’s the best” or “You’re the best,” depending on context.
Means “of the best/top” and is used before a noun (e.g., 최고의 영화).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 이 식당은 우리 동네에서 최고의 식당이에요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This restaurant is the best restaurant in our neighborhood.
Recently, I’ve had too much work.

definitions.native: as much as possible, to the greatest extent
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’ll finish as quickly as possible.

definitions.note: Object form of 최선, used with verbs like 다하다 (to do).
Informal/polite 해체 form; often used to congratulate someone (e.g., for a birthday, graduation, good news).
Polite speech level (해요체); used to congratulate someone.
Informal/polite present tense of 출발하다 (used in casual conversation).
Often used with places or institutions (e.g., 서울 출신 “from Seoul”, 연세대 출신 “a Yonsei graduate”).
‘춤’ means “dance,” and ‘-을’ is the object particle (marks it as the direct object).
-고 connects to the next verb/action; it often means “and” or “and then.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My friends listen to music, dance, and sing.

definitions.note: This is the noun 충격 with the object particle -을 attached.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 그 소식을 듣고 큰 충격을 받았어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I was very shocked when I heard the news.

definitions.note: Used with the object particle 를/을 to mark what is being given or received as advice.
Attributive form of 충분하다 used before a noun.
Informal/polite spoken style of 충분하다 (used to say something is enough).
Often used before a verb or adjective to mean “enough / sufficiently.”
Casual past tense of 추다, used in informal speech (often to friends).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Yesterday, I danced with my friends.

definitions.note: verb form of 치다 used to modify a following noun (like “hitting/striking …”)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I can hear Minsu hitting the ball.

definitions.note: Used for medical treatment/therapy.
Informal/plain command form of 치우다 (used when telling someone to do it).
-가 is the subject marker attached to 친구 (“friend”).

definitions.native: as for a friend, (my/your/etc.) friend (topic marker)
definitions.note: 친구 + 는: ‘는’ marks ‘friend’ as the topic of the sentence.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: As for my friend, they are at school now.

definitions.note: Plural form of 친구; -들 is a common plural marker.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I'm going to go watch a movie with my friends.

definitions.note: "-들은" marks the plural topic (friends + as for).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My friends are at school now.

definitions.note: Plural with 들 + subject/topic particle 이 (used after a consonant).
Includes the object particle 를, marking ‘friend’ as the direct object of the verb.
Informal way to call/address a friend (친구 + vocative particle 야).
A poetic/vocative form used to directly address a friend (like “O friend”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My friend, listen to what I’m saying.

definitions.note: Polite present tense of 친구이다; used in statements like “X is a friend.”
Uses the particle 와 meaning “with” after a noun.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I eat lunch together with a friend.

definitions.note: plain (dictionary-style) present form; used in statements, writing, or talking to oneself

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I want to sleep in bed.

definitions.native: on the bed, in the bed
definitions.note: -에 is a location particle meaning “on/in/at.” With 침대 (bed), it often translates as “on/in bed” depending on context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I lay down on the bed.

definitions.note: 침대 means “bed” and -에서 marks the location where something is or happens.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I read a book in bed.

definitions.note: Informal/polite style (해요체) form of 침착하다, used to describe someone being calm or to tell someone to calm down (depending on context).
Commonly used for things like a credit card, membership card, ID card, or game card.

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I peeled an apple with a knife.

definitions.note: Topic form: 칼 + 은. Used to mark “knife” as the topic of the sentence.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: As for the knife, it’s sharp.

definitions.note: Used for the weight/purity of gemstones (e.g., diamonds).
A loanword; commonly used for the captain/leader of a sports team.
informal/polite-neutral style (해체) present form of 크다; used as a sentence ending meaning “(it) is big.”

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I drink coffee in the morning.

definitions.note: ‘커피를’ is ‘coffee’ with the object particle -를.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I drink coffee in the morning.

definitions.note: Commonly used in Konglish, especially in tech, games, or sports (e.g., controlling a device, character, or situation).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This game has difficult character controls.

definitions.note: ‘는’ is a topic marker attached to the noun.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The computer is on the desk.

definitions.note: ‘를’ is the object particle attached to ‘컴퓨터’.
Direct-object form of 케이크 with the object particle 를.
Often used for things like computer code, a password/PIN, or a barcode/QR code.
Object-marked form of 코드 (with 를). Often used for computer code or other codes (e.g., QR code, access code).
Object form of 코트 (used with 를).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It was cold, so I wore a coat.

definitions.note: Adverb form of 크다 (“to be big”), meaning “in a big way,” often used for things like speaking loudly, writing big, or increasing a lot.
Attributive form of 크다 used before a noun (e.g. 큰 집 = “a big house”).
Can mean a nightlife club, a school/group club, or a sports club (loanword).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I went to a club with my friends on the weekend.

definitions.note: 키 is “height” (or “key” in other contexts), but with the subject marker -가 here it means “height (as the subject).”
Informal/polite spoken style (해체) of 키스하다; used with someone close or in casual situations.
From 키우다 (“to raise/grow”); 키우고 is the connective form meaning “and (then) raise/grow” or “while raising/growing.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I raise a puppy and also raise a cat.

definitions.note: Casual/informal form (often used with friends or in spoken Korean); it can also be used when telling someone to raise/grow something.
Commonly used for riding/boarding vehicles (bus, taxi, subway, etc.).
Connected form of 타다 with -고, used to link actions ("and then").
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I took the bus and went to school.

definitions.note: From 타다. Depending on context it can mean 'that is riding (in/on)' or 'that is burning' (e.g., 타는 버스 = the bus you're riding; 타는 불 = burning fire).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 저는 지금 타는 버스를 기다리고 있어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m waiting for the bus I’m going to ride right now.

definitions.note: Past attributive form of 타다, used to describe a noun (e.g., 'the bus I rode').
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The bus I rode just arrived.

definitions.note: Future/intent attributive form of 타다, used before a noun (e.g. 탈 버스 = “the bus (I) will ride”).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 제가 오늘 탈 버스가 곧 와요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The bus I'm going to ride today is coming soon.

definitions.note: Used for getting on a vehicle (plane, train, bus, etc.). Here it’s the object form with 을.
past attributive form of 태어나다; used to describe a noun (e.g., "a person who was born in...")
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I am a person who was born in Korea.

definitions.note: casual/informal past tense (spoken style)
Includes the object particle -를 (“(the) taxi/cab” as the direct object of a verb).

definitions.native: so, since (I will / it seems / I think)
definitions.note: Sentence ending meaning roughly “(because) I will…” or “(because) I think it will…,” often used to give a reason before a request, suggestion, or instruction.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 제가 먼저 갈 테니까 걱정하지 마세요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’ll go first, so don’t worry.

definitions.note: Colloquial/polite sentence ending from -(으)ㄹ 테니까요, used to give a reason based on the speaker’s intention or promise (often implying “so please … / don’t worry”).

definitions.native: I wonder if…, could it be that…?
definitions.note: A sentence-ending form used after a verb/adjective with -(으)ㄹ (as in -(으)ㄹ 텐가) to express wondering or a rhetorical question.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I wonder if it will rain.

definitions.note: Used after a verb/adjective stem to express the speaker’s guess or expectation, often followed by -는데 to add a contrasting or explanatory tone (like “so…” or “but…”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You’re probably busy right now, so I’ll call you later.

definitions.note: Contraction of 터인데. Used after a verb/adjective to show the speaker’s guess/expectation and then add a result, suggestion, or contrast in the next clause.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It will probably rain, so take an umbrella.

definitions.note: Common loanword used for music, sports, and general rhythm/speed.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Let’s slow down the workout pace a little today.

definitions.note: “토끼가” means “rabbit” with the subject marker 가 (used when 토끼 is the subject of the sentence).
The topic particle -는 is attached to 토끼 to mean “as for the rabbit / the rabbit (topic)”.
‘를’ marks 토끼 as the direct object of the verb.

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This glass cup is pretty transparent.
A truck is driving on the road.
Today is a special day for me.

definitions.note: Object form of 특허 (used with the object particle -를).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 그는 새로운 기술에 대한 특허를 냈어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He filed a patent for a new technology.

definitions.note: Casual/informal past form (to a close friend or someone younger).
Casual/informal past tense of 틀리다; often used to say someone is incorrect or an answer is wrong.
Used to express strong confidence that something is true or will happen.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 그 사람은 틀림없이 내일 올 거예요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: That person will definitely come tomorrow.

definitions.native: as for the team, the team (topic)
definitions.note: "팀" (team) + topic particle "은" (marks the topic; often translated as "as for").
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: As for the team, there is a game tomorrow.

definitions.note: Subject/topic form of 팀 with the particle -이.
Direct object form of 팁 (with the object particle -을). Often used for tipping at restaurants, cafés, etc.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I gave a tip because you served us.

definitions.note: Attributive form of 팔다 used to modify a noun (e.g., ‘the person who is selling …’).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I went to a store that sells bread.

definitions.note: used before a noun (attributive form of 파랗다)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The blue sky is really pretty today.

definitions.note: Direct object form of 파이 (marked with 를).
‘파일을’ is ‘파일’ (file) + the object particle ‘-을’.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please send the file by email.

definitions.note: Used for a business/work partner, a romantic partner, or someone you do something with (e.g., in a game or project).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m working on this project together with a partner.

definitions.note: The subject form of 파트너 (partner) with the particle -가.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My partner comes to the meeting today.

definitions.note: ‘파티를’ is the object form of 파티 (used with 를 after a vowel).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: We had a party on the weekend.

definitions.note: -에 marks a location/time and is often translated as “at” or “to” depending on context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m going to go to a party this evening.

definitions.note: Sino-Korean number used in counting (팔, 구, 십...)
This is 팔 (arm) with the object particle 을.
The subject-marked form of 팔 (“arm”), with the subject particle -이.
Most often means a fan of a celebrity/team; can also mean an electric fan, depending on context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I'm a fan of this singer.

definitions.note: Commonly spelled "판다" in standard Korean; "팬더" is also used.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I saw a panda at the zoo.

definitions.note: This is 펜 with the object particle -을 attached.
Often used for episodes of TV shows, dramas, YouTube series, etc.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This drama has come out up to episode 3 now.

definitions.note: Used with people to mean which side they are on (e.g., my side vs. your side).
Casual/informal speech (to a friend). Often used like “나는 네 편이야.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Don’t worry, I’m on your side.

definitions.native: is easier, is more comfortable, is more convenient
definitions.note: Casual/informal speech (to a friend). Often used in comparisons like “A가 B보다 편이야.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The bus is more convenient than the subway.

definitions.note: Usually a written letter/message (often on paper), not a “letter” of the alphabet.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I wrote a letter to my grandmother.

definitions.note: This is 편지 with the object particle -를 (used after a vowel).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I write a letter to a friend.

definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 그는 편집증 때문에 사람들을 쉽게 믿지 못해요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Because of paranoia, he can't easily trust people.

definitions.note: Attributive form of 평범하다; used before a noun.
Often used with expressions like 평생 동안 (“for a lifetime”).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 저는 평생 이 도시에서 살 거예요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I will live in this city for my whole life.

definitions.note: “평화가” is “평화” (peace) + the subject particle “-가”.
Object form of 평화, used with object particles like -를/-을.

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: There’s an abandoned house up in the mountains over there.

definitions.note: a respectful title used to address a king, queen, or emperor/empress
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Your Majesty, your subjects are waiting outside.

definitions.note: Informal/polite style (해요체) form, commonly used in casual conversation.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If it’s too hard, it’s okay to give up.

definitions.note: Short for 휴대폰 (“mobile phone”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Can you lend me your phone for a moment?

definitions.note: Informal/polite style ending (-아/어). Used for commands (“solve it”), suggestions (“let’s solve it”), or in connected speech (“and then solve…”), depending on context.
프랑스어 + topic marker 는 (“as for…”, “regarding…”)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: As for French, the pronunciation is a bit difficult.

definitions.note: 프랑스어 (French language) + 로 (in/with/by); used to mean “in French” (e.g., when saying or writing something in French).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please translate this sentence into French.

definitions.note: ‘프랑스어를’ is ‘프랑스어’ with the object particle -를 (used after a vowel).
Commonly used for TV/radio programs, software/computer programs, and event schedules.
피 (blood) + 가, the subject marker meaning “blood” is the subject of the sentence.
Object form of 피 (blood). It’s used before verbs like “to draw/take,” “to see,” etc.

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I want to play the piano.

definitions.note: ‘를’ is an object particle meaning ‘(the) piano’ as the direct object of a verb.
Commonly used with the negative ending -지 않다 (e.g., 피우지 않아요 = “I don’t smoke”).
Conjugated form of 피하다; often used as a command (“Avoid it.”) or in casual speech.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 비 오는 날은 이 길을 피해.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Avoid this road on rainy days.
Water is really necessary for us.

definitions.note: ‘-가’ is the subject marker attached to ‘필요’ (“need”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Right now, I don't need a rest.

definitions.note: Often used with a subject/topic marker (이/가) to say something is needed/necessary; also common with ~가 필요해요/필요합니다 in polite speech.

definitions.native: (that it is) necessary, (that it is) needed
definitions.note: Used to report or quote someone’s opinion with -다고 (e.g., “(someone says/thinks) it’s necessary”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The doctor said that surgery is necessary.

definitions.note: polite (honorific) form, used when speaking to or about someone of higher status
Commonly used in casual speech as a shortened form of 필요하지요/필요하죠 (“it is necessary/needed,” often with a confirming tone like “right?”).
Attributive form of 필요하다 used before a noun.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I packed only the things I needed.

definitions.note: From 필요하다; this form is used before a noun or to connect to another phrase (e.g., 필요할 때 = “when needed”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Call me when you need help.

definitions.note: Polite formal present tense.
Informal polite style ending (-해). Used to say something is needed/necessary.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Right now, I need a rest.

definitions.note: Polite present tense (해요체) of 필요하다.
An interjection used to express a light laugh, a small exclamation, or a brief reaction (like “ha!”).
Imperative in the older/formal 하게체 speech style, often used by an older person to someone younger or lower-ranking.
Used as the auxiliary 하다 in reported-speech patterns like -다고 하고 / -라고 하고 (“say that…”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He said he would come tomorrow and left.

definitions.note: Used to connect actions/verbs (the “-고” form).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I do my homework and then sleep.

definitions.note: Shortened form of "하기를" (nominalized "하다" + object particle). Commonly used in patterns like "하길 바라(요)" = "hope (you) do it".
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I hope you do your homework in advance.

definitions.note: native Korean number (used for counting); often shortened to 한 before a noun (e.g., 한 개 = one item).
Used after a verb/adjective clause (often with -까) to express wondering/uncertainty.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I wonder if he will come today.

definitions.note: ‘하나’ (one) with the subject marker ‘-가’ attached.
Usually used with a negative verb to mean “not even one / not at all.”
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 저는 오늘 아무것도 하나도 안 먹었어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I didn’t eat anything at all today.

definitions.note: object-marked form of 하나 (“one”) with 를
-만 means “only/just” and attaches to 하나 (“one”).
formal polite question form used after a verb stem to ask what someone does/is doing
Used before a noun to mean “a/one” or “one of the …” (as in “one of the reasons”).
Informal ending (-네) used when the speaker notices or realizes something (often with mild surprise).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Oh, you're already doing your homework.

definitions.note: Attributive form of 하다 used to modify a following noun (like “doing …” / “… that does”).
Present attributive (modifier) form of 하다, used before a noun.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The work I do is interesting.

definitions.note: Often links to the next clause with a contrasting or background meaning ("but/though"), or sets up what comes next ("and then").
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I'm busy right now, but I'll call you later.

definitions.note: A common connective meaning “but/though” or “and/so” depending on context. It links to what comes next and often sets up contrast or background.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 저는 열심히 공부하는데 성적이 안 올라요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I study hard, but my grades don’t go up.

definitions.note: Used to express uncertainty or to ask indirectly (e.g., ‘whether …’). Often appears before verbs like 알다/모르다/궁금하다.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 그 사람이 왜 그렇게 하는지 모르겠어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I don't know why that person does that.
The sky is really blue today.

definitions.note: Often used with the informal ending “-니?” to ask a question (casual).
Adnominal (noun-modifying) form of 하다. Often refers to something you were doing before (sometimes unfinished or interrupted).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I finished what I was doing.

definitions.note: Often used with 하다 (e.g., ~도록 하다) to give an instruction or to make sure something is done.
Used to quote or convey a command/instruction like “(someone) said/told (me/you/them) to do (it).”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The teacher told us to do our homework.

definitions.note: Used to quote a command/order (하다 + -라고). Often followed by verbs like 하다/말하다/시키다 (e.g., 하라고 했어요 = 'told (me) to do it').
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My mom told me to do my homework.

definitions.note: used to express purpose, often followed by 가다/오다 (go/come)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I go to the park to exercise.

definitions.note: Used after a verb stem to express purpose or intention (e.g., 하려고 = “(in order) to do / intending to do”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I went to the park to exercise.

definitions.note: From 하다 + -(으)려는; it modifies a following noun (e.g., “a person who is trying to…”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please don’t stop someone who is trying to leave now.
I drink eight glasses of water a day.
Today I was at home all day.

definitions.note: Conditional form of 하다 used to mean “if (you/I/they) do (it)” depending on context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If you do your homework, you can play.

definitions.note: -면 conditional form of 하다 (“to do”); often used to mean “if you do (it)” or “when you do (it)”.
